sum: AstraZeneca Pharma share price today: Shares of AstraZeneca Pharma India rallied 7% in early trading on Friday, November 6, after the pharmaceutical company reported year-on-year (YoY) growth in revenue, EBITDA and net profit for the second quarter of FY27.
As of 9:33 AM, AstraZeneca Pharma shares had touched an intraday high of Rs 6,801, compared with the previous closing price of Rs 6,294, representing a gain of approximately 8.1% at the day's high.
AstraZeneca Pharma reported standalone revenue of Rs 729 crore in Q2 FY27, registering a 30.4% YoY increase compared with Rs 559 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
The company's net profit rose 14.9% YoY to Rs 62.3 crore from Rs 54.2 crore in Q2 FY26.

However, the EBITDA margin contracted to 13% from 13.4%, reflecting a decline of 40 basis points.

items.t: AstraZeneca offers $10B to buy drugmaker Rhythm
sum: ASTRAZENECA made an offer of about $10 billion to acquire obesity drugmaker Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, according to three people familiar with the matter.
AstraZeneca offered as much as $134 a share in the nonbinding proposal, including payments for milestone achievements, the people said.
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Wednesday that AstraZeneca had made a $124-per-share offer for the company last month.
Shares of Rhythm closed up 28 percent at $110.68 on the news, giving it a market capitalization of about $7.64 billion.

The acquisition would be pursued through AstraZeneca’s rare-disease business Alexion, which the company acquired for $39 billion in 2021 to expand beyond its core oncology and biopharmaceutical franchises, two of the people said.
AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot is seeking to shift investors’ focus back to growth after a few turbulent months.
The company, which has a $292-billion market value, faced some clinical trial setbacks, and reports of a potentially transformative deal with US rival Bristol Myers Squibb had weighed on the shares.

Why Is AstraZeneca (LSE:AZN) Stock Still Climbing After Its Latest Quarterly Results?
sum: - AstraZeneca reported quarterly revenue and core earnings ahead of market forecasts, with oncology, respiratory and rare disease franchises offsetting older-drug erosion.
- Full-year guidance was reconfirmed and management described next year as unusually rich in late-stage pipeline readouts.
- A multi-year reshaping programme aimed at sustainable growth was announced alongside the numbers, keeping the FTSE 100 pharma leader at the centre of healthcare stock conversations.

AstraZeneca (LSE:AZN) Healthcare AstraZeneca PLC (LSE:AZN) 12822.00 GBX -32.000 0.249% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T16:36:00Z remains one of the most closely watched healthcare stocks in London this week after its latest quarterly results landed ahead of expectations and sent the shares sharply higher. The Cambridge-based group reported revenue growth across its main therapy areas, with core earnings rising faster than sales as margins improved and the business absorbed the loss of exclusivity on some of its older medicines. The development is being closely followed by investors tracking UK Healthcare Stocks.

The reaction in the market was emphatic, with the shares jumping on the day and holding most of those gains into the start of this week. For a company that had drifted earlier in the year on worries about pricing pressure and Chinese procurement, the update offered a reminder of how much momentum sits inside its newer launches.

Oncology was once again the engine of the quarter. Enhertu, Imfinzi, Calquence and Tagrisso all grew strongly, and alliance revenue from partnered antibody-drug conjugates rose at a rapid clip. Respiratory and immunology medicines such as Tezspire, Saphnelo and Breztri delivered solid growth, while in rare disease the conversion of patients from Soliris to Ultomiris continued to support the franchise even as biosimilar competition arrived.

Those gains more than offset declines in Farxiga and Brilinta, which have lost exclusivity in key markets, and the ongoing effect of volume-based procurement in China. Management said that stripping out the medicines facing generic competition, underlying growth was considerably faster than the headline rate.

Earnings roundup: AstraZeneca’s cost cuts, Alnylam’s slump and Regeneron’s resilience
sum: With quarterly earnings underway, BioPharma Dive is providing a snapshot of some companies' results and how they're being received by investors. Today, we're offering insight into the latest numbers from AstraZeneca, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals.

Since 2024, AstraZeneca has zeroed in on a key number: $80 billion. Executives have been adamant full-year revenue will hit that target by 2030, even in the face of multiple clinical setbacks that have slowed the company's momentum.

AstraZeneca reiterated in its latest earnings report it is "on track" to meet that goal. Since February, the company has reported positive results from 12 late-stage programs and brought four new drugs to market, CEO Pascal Soriot told analysts. Over the next year, 20 "high-value trial readouts" could, if positive, yield peak annual revenue opportunities surpassing $20 billion.
"A significant part" of that total should "become reality over the next few years," Soriot proclaimed.

Yet a different number — $1.5 billion — caught Wall Street's attention on Friday. That's a figure associated with a new cost-savings program, "Reshaping for Sustainable Growth," that AstraZeneca revealed alongside its June-to-September results. Through it, the company will save $1.5 billion annually and "reinvest" that money largely back into drug research, according to a presentation.

When speaking with analysts, CEO Soriot claimed AstraZeneca has been working on this plan since the beginning of the year. The company believes it has to "redeploy resources" to support its pipeline, in part by embedding artificial intelligence more deeply into its operations, he said.
AI is helping "make us faster, smarter," Soriot said. AstraZeneca can "grow without growing," meaning it can "grow without adding as many people as you would have if you didn't have the use of AI."

FTSE 100 Rises to 10,729.78 as AstraZeneca and BT Offset NatWest's Slump
sum: London's blue-chip index outperformed most global markets on Friday 30 October 2026, with pharmaceutical, telecoms and energy heavyweights cushioning a sharp fall in NatWest and a global technology selloff.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,729.78 on Friday 30 October 2026, up 7.71 points or 0.07% from Thursday's close of 10,722.07. London's index opened higher and rose about 0.5% in the first hour of trade, according to InstaForex, before giving back most of that advance as the global technology selloff deepened and Wall Street opened sharply lower. The small gain was nonetheless enough to secure the FTSE 100's first monthly rise in three months.

The index's resilience stands out on a day when Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 2%, Nasdaq futures dropped more than 2% and Germany's DAX 40 retreated. The FTSE 100's heavy weighting toward pharmaceuticals, energy, consumer staples and mining, and its relatively light exposure to technology, has made it a natural refuge during the latest bout of AI-related selling.

AstraZeneca, one of the three largest companies in the index, was among the leading risers after reporting third-quarter revenue of $16,209 million, up 7% at constant exchange rates, and core earnings per share of $2.79, up 19% at constant exchange rates. The drugmaker reaffirmed its full-year guidance and announced a restructuring programme expected to save around $1.5 billion, which it said would support long-term ambitions including investment in new drug pipelines.

AstraZeneca shares closed about 7% higher, the stock's best day in a year according to Reuters reporting, and GSK added around 2.5%. The broader pharmaceutical sector gained 5.1% over October, its biggest monthly rise since February. Because AstraZeneca carries such a large index weighting, its rally alone more than offset the losses in banks and miners.

NatWest Group was the biggest drag on the index and the worst performer in the STOXX 600, closing nearly 9% lower after its third-quarter net interest income fell short of analyst expectations. The bank reported attributable profit of £1,532 million and operating pre-tax profit of £2.23 billion, up from £2.18 billion a year earlier, with total income of £4.64 billion.

AstraZeneca Q3 Revenue Rises 7%, $1.5 Billion Cost-Cutting Plan Lifts Shares Over 5% Pre-Market
sum: TradingKey is a comprehensive financial markets platform dedicated to equipping investors and traders with the tools and insights they need. TradingKey's mission is to empower you to make smarter, more informed decisions.

TradingKey - On October 30, AstraZeneca (AZN) stock rose over 5% in pre-market trading. The company's third-quarter revenue and earnings both exceeded market expectations, while it reaffirmed its full-year guidance and announced a restructuring plan expected to deliver $1.5 billion in annual benefits, boosting investor confidence in its medium- to long-term growth prospects.

At constant exchange rates, AstraZeneca's total third-quarter revenue increased 7% year-over-year to $16.209 billion, exceeding market expectations of approximately $16 billion. Product sales grew 5% to $15.066 billion, while alliance revenue surged 36% to $1.107 billion. Core earnings per share were $2.79, up 19% year-over-year and about 7% above the market expectation of approximately $2.60; reported EPS rose 26% to $2.02.

The oncology business remained the primary growth engine, with third-quarter revenue growing 17% year-over-year to $7.77 billion. Sales of breast cancer drug Enhertu rose 35% to $969 million, and immunotherapy Imfinzi revenue grew 26% to approximately $2 billion, helping the company offset generic competition pressures on mature products. Meanwhile, sales of diabetes drug Farxiga fell 25% to $1.61 billion.

Beyond financial performance, market attention also turned to AstraZeneca's R&D pipeline. CEO Pascal Soriot stated that the company currently has over 180 R&D projects, and a series of clinical trials expected to report results in 2027 has a combined peak annual sales potential exceeding $20 billion. Multiple late-stage R&D assets covering oncology, respiratory diseases, and rare diseases provide support for achieving the company's 2030 revenue targets.

To create room for increased R&D investment, AstraZeneca simultaneously launched a "Reshaping for Sustainable Growth" initiative. The project is expected to be largely completed by the end of 2029, generating approximately $1.5 billion in annual pre-tax run-rate benefits, with funds primarily reinvested into the drug pipeline and new technologies.

Olema Pharmaceuticals Shares Fall 15.1% Following AstraZeneca SERENA-4 Trial Results
sum: Olema Pharmaceuticals (NASDAQ:OLMA) shares fell 15.1% in pre-market trading to $8.68 after AstraZeneca reported that its Phase 3 SERENA-4 trial of camizestrant did not meet its primary endpoint.

AstraZeneca said on Friday that camizestrant, in combination with palbociclib, did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in progression-free survival as a first-line treatment for patients with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer.
Investors were assessing the result in relation to Olema's lead candidate, palazestrant (OP-1250), which is being evaluated in the pivotal Phase 3 OPERA-01 trial.
Palazestrant is an oral selective estrogen receptor degrader and complete estrogen receptor antagonist, or SERD/CERAN.
Its mechanism therefore has similarities to camizestrant, although the outcome of AstraZeneca's trial does not determine the results of Olema's separate clinical programme.
According to the supplied information, the SERENA-4 result follows Roche's persevERA trial earlier in 2026, which also did not meet its objective in the first-line advanced breast cancer setting.
Following the AstraZeneca results, Stifel reduced its price target for Olema to $30 from $48 while maintaining a Buy rating.

sum: AstraZeneca stock (ISIN US6549022043) is trading broadly steady as investors digest a new exclusive licensing agreement for a Lipoprotein(a) inhibitor announced on September 13, 2026. The move comes on the back of recently reported quarterly figures that showed solid revenue growth and a maintained guidance range for 2026.

According to StockStar on September 13, 2026, AstraZeneca entered into an exclusive licensing agreement with CSPC Pharmaceutical Group to develop, manufacture and commercialize the Lipoprotein(a) inhibitor candidate YS2302018 globally. The agreement covers YS2302018 and any subsequent medicines or biologics derived from this compound, signalling AstraZeneca's intention to strengthen its cardiovascular portfolio.

While financial terms were not disclosed in the available summary, the deal adds a late-stage or potentially mid-stage asset targeting elevated Lipoprotein(a), a known risk factor for cardiovascular events. For investors, the key question is how quickly YS2302018 can progress through clinical development and whether it will complement AstraZeneca's existing cardiovascular drugs.

In its most recent reported quarter for 2026, AstraZeneca posted higher revenue compared with the same period a year earlier, with total revenue in the quarter rising to a mid-teens billion dollar figure and representing a year-on-year increase in the low double-digit percent range, as indicated by the latest investor materials linked from AstraZeneca. For context, this quarterly performance forms part of a broader trend in which AstraZeneca has delivered consistent revenue growth across its main therapy areas.

The same quarterly update confirmed that core earnings per share remained on an upward trajectory year-on-year, driven by growth in oncology and cardiovascular medicines, while the company reiterated full-year 2026 guidance ranges for revenue and core EPS. items.t: AstraZeneca Shares Tick Higher After €2.55bn Bond Offering
sum: Shares in AstraZeneca (LON: AZN) edged higher on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, after the pharmaceutical giant announced it had successfully priced a €2.55 billion bond offering through its wholly owned subsidiary, AstraZeneca Finance LLC.

The four-tranche Eurobond issuance, priced on 24 August 2026 and expected to close on 1 September 2026, is being carried out under the group’s Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) programme. The Notes will be admitted to the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s Official List and traded on the London Stock Exchange’s Main Market.

The offering comprises €700 million of notes carrying a 3.402% coupon maturing in March 2030, €600 million at 3.652% maturing in September 2032, €500 million at 3.923% maturing in September 2035, and €750 million at 4.169% maturing in September 2038. All tranches are fully and unconditionally guaranteed by AstraZeneca PLC.

The company said the move is aligned with its “long-term funding strategy,” with net proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes. Barclays Bank, Goldman Sachs International and Morgan Stanley acted as joint book-running managers on the transaction.
Investors appeared to welcome the news as a sign of continued balance sheet management and access to favourable debt markets, helping nudge the shares modestly higher in early trading.

The staggered maturities, stretching from 2030 to 2038, suggest AstraZeneca is locking in financing across a range of tenors, potentially supporting future investment in its drug pipeline and ongoing expansion plans.
The Notes have not been registered under the US Securities Act and cannot be offered or sold within the United States absent an applicable exemption.

items.t: AstraZeneca Shares Drop on Report of Potential Merger Talks with Bristol Myers Squibb
sum: AstraZeneca PLC (LSE:AZN) shares fell almost 7% in London trading after reports emerged that the pharmaceutical company has held discussions with Bristol-Myers Squibb Company (NYSE:BMY) regarding a potential merger. If completed, the transaction would create one of the world's largest drugmakers, with a combined market value approaching $400 billion.

AstraZeneca's shares declined 6.7% to 11,804 pence, while the FTSE 100 traded little changed. In the U.S., Bristol Myers Squibb rose 2.7% in pre-market trading after ending Friday's session at $65.31, close to its highest level in the past 52 weeks.

Based on current market valuations, a combined company would be worth nearly $400 billion. AstraZeneca has a market capitalisation of around $264 billion, while Bristol Myers Squibb is valued at approximately $133 billion.

According to a report by the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, merger discussions have taken place over recent months. However, the report noted that negotiations remain preliminary and could ultimately be delayed or fail to result in an agreement. Neither company has publicly commented on the report, and no details regarding a possible transaction structure have been disclosed.
The reported discussions come at a time when both companies are pursuing ambitious growth strategies.

Under Chief Executive Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca has transformed into one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies after rejecting Pfizer's $118 billion takeover proposal in 2014. More recently, the company announced plans to invest $50 billion in U.S. manufacturing and research facilities while outlining its intention to pursue a direct U.S. stock market listing to broaden access to American investors.

For Bristol Myers Squibb, acquisitions have become an increasingly important part of its strategy as it seeks to strengthen its product pipeline ahead of upcoming patent expiries. The company has continued to expand its oncology and immunology portfolio through partnerships and business development initiatives, making a larger strategic combination a potential avenue for accelerating long-term growth.

AstraZeneca Shares Drop Following Wainua’s Failed Heart Disease Trial
sum: - Extensive background and on-study uptake of TTR stabilizers likely diluted the observable marginal effect of a TTR-silencing agent, complicating attribution of benefit in the intent-to-treat primary analysis.
- Nominally significant signal in patients not receiving stabilizers highlights a potential efficacy subset, but it is insufficient to rescue a failed primary endpoint in a registrational framework.

AstraZeneca's Wainua failed to meet the primary endpoint of a late-stage trial in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy, sending shares down nearly 10% in their largest single-day decline since late 2024.

AstraZeneca's Wainua, a nerve disease drug developed in partnership with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, failed to meet the primary endpoint of a late-stage trial in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy.

The failure sent AstraZeneca shares down nearly 10% while also raising questions about the company's clinical trial design capabilities. In the trial, the drug did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular deaths and recurring heart problems when added to standard care in the 140-week trial, which enrolled 1,432 patients.1

Analysts pointed quickly to trial design as a central issue. In the study, 57% of patients were already taking a stabilizer, drugs such as Pfizer's Vyndaqel that work by stabilizing the faulty proteins that accumulate in the heart, and a further 24% added a stabilizer during the study period. Wainua, like Alnylam's Amvuttra, works by reducing production of those proteins rather than stabilizing them, making the co-administration of the two drug classes difficult to disentangle in assessing Wainua's benefit.

AstraZeneca noted that taking Wainua as a standalone therapy without stabilizers showed "nominally significant" benefit, but the primary endpoint, which included patients on combination therapy, was not met.2

AstraZeneca stock drops 9% after heart drug trial miss deals rare blow to pharma powerhouse
sum: Shares of AstraZeneca fell as much as 9% after a late-stage clinical trial for a heart disease drug failed to meet its target, with analysts saying the bigger issue may be investors' trust in the company rather than the loss of a few extra billion in sales.

Wainua – a medicine AstraZeneca had been testing on whether it could help patients with a rare heart condition – did not reach its main goal of reducing deaths and recurrent heart-related emergencies over 140 weeks compared to a placebo, the British drugmaker said in a press release early Thursday.

It examined how the medicine could help patients with a rare, life-threatening heart condition called transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy, or ATTR cardiomyopathy, when added to a patient's current treatment plan

Jefferies analysts said the result didn't jeopardise the company's $80 billion sales target by 2030 but noted that AstraZeneca "had been very confident around the primary endpoint and the ability to hit in combination use."

"The bigger issue is probably a degree of credibility loss with management being very confident in the trial's ability to hit the primary endpoint as well as an ability to show utility on top of background therapy," the analysts said, modeling for $2.5 billion less in risk-adjusted sales for the medicine.

Under CEO Pascal Soriot's leadership over the past 14 years, AstraZeneca has developed a reputation as a steadfast powerhouse, especially in oncology. It rarely posts negative trial results, and Thursday's surprise disappointment may have ripple effects beyond the medicine itself.

AstraZeneca confirmed that its existing license for Wainua was unaffected by these trial results. The drug is already approved for treating conditions where misfolded proteins build up, causing nerve damage. It is sold in Europe as Wainzua.

AstraZeneca (LSE:AZN) Healthcare AstraZeneca PLC (LSE:AZN) 12822.00 GBX -32.000 0.249% Last Updated at: 2026-10-27T16:36:00Z remained a central name in the UK healthcare conversation as the FTSE 100 traded close to record ground, with market participants weighing how the pharmaceutical heavyweight fits into a session where mining and financial shares set much of the tone.

AstraZeneca (AZN) is one of the largest members of the FTSE 100 and a bellwether for the UK pharmaceutical space, so its shares are closely tracked whenever sentiment around the sector shifts. The group develops and markets medicines across oncology, respiratory, cardiovascular and rare disease areas, and its scale means it often anchors discussions about defensive positioning. On a day when the broader index leaned on cyclical strength, attention turned to whether large, earnings-durable healthcare names would keep pace or lag a market being pulled higher by resources and banks.

The FTSE 100 has been pressing toward record ground, helped by firmer mining shares, resilient financials, easing tensions in the Middle East and steadier readings on the UK economy. In such a setting, cyclical sectors frequently attract flows first, while defensive groups such as pharmaceuticals can trade more quietly. For a company of AstraZeneca's size, this dynamic shapes how its shares are perceived relative to the index, since large healthcare names can act as ballast when sentiment turns cautious yet may draw less attention during a broad risk-on advance.
